A national LGBTI human-rights organisation's 24th annual report (March 2026) identifies this state/province as the one where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 - up approximately 150 % year-on-year - during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). Formal trans visibility here is extremely low: only 157 people used the national gender-identity law for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. The organisation interprets the pattern as a decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

This state/province sits below the country-wide average by a modest, trend-driven margin rather than through any specific incident. There is no trans-specific indigenous customary-law jurisdiction and no documented state-implicated violence here; the indigenous-people note is structural context within a state/province under prolonged security conflict. Compared with the neighbouring state/province carrying a concrete judicial annulment finding, this state/province is marginally safer: its problem is a statistical acceleration from a low base, not a court ruling naming trans women as outside the femicide definition. Compared with the neighbouring state/province where over half the national case load concentrates, this state/province is clearly safer despite the 150 % rise, because its absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising state/province with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.
